walkthroughs.body_html:
Foundations of Environmental Systems — a core area of Environmental Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Foundations of Environmental Systems brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Foundations of Environmental Systems.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

Why is burning fossil fuels considered to disrupt the carbon cycle?
options: It releases carbon stored for millions of years much faster than the cycle can absorb.
It creates new carbon that did not exist before.
It removes carbon permanently.
Rainforests are deserts most of the year.

mcqs.q: Why are tropical rainforest soils often nutrient-poor despite abundant vegetation?
options: Rainforests have rich soils because they are productive.
Rainforests are deserts most of the year.
Rapid decomposition and uptake mean nutrients cycle quickly through living biomass, not soil.
It removes carbon permanently.

mcqs.q: How does the Brundtland Report define sustainable development?
options: Stopping all development immediately.
Rainforests are deserts most of the year.
Meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs.
Environmental protection at all costs.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Precautionary principle”?
options: Meeting present needs without compromising ability of future generations to meet theirs (Brundtland 1987).
Worldview shaping how individuals/societies evaluate environmental issues; ecocentric, anthropocentric, technocentric (IBDP categorisation).
Analysing environment as interlinked open systems with inputs, outputs, flows, feedbacks.
Where serious damage threatens, lack of full scientific certainty should not delay preventive action.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Sustainability”?
options: Individual rational use of shared resource leads to collective ruin (Hardin 1968 in Science).
Meeting present needs without compromising ability of future generations to meet theirs (Brundtland 1987).
Analysing environment as interlinked open systems with inputs, outputs, flows, feedbacks.
Where serious damage threatens, lack of full scientific certainty should not delay preventive action.
